<reason>Side A built a tighter, more consistently defended case around a single clean frame: bonuses let cities "price" the upzone (extract below-market units, fees, siting requirements) while a blanket ban legally guarantees nothing and universalizes speculative pressure on affordable starter homes ("windfall now, filtering trickle later"). A's rebuttals directly engaged B's language, answered both pressure questions with clean A1/A2 structure, and landed a genuine logical trap on B's permit/veto distinction (either ministerial review blocks cumulative load, meaning the "fight" B claims to eliminate still exists, or it can't, meaning the ban legalizes overload) that B's closing never squarely resolved. Side B's structural point about discretionary vetoes and its Minneapolis/Auckland examples were strong and original, but B leaned on filtering theory and repeated city references rather than directly rebutting A's specific mechanism about near-term displacement of affordable stock, and never fully closed the trap A sprang in R2. B's opening was also clipped for exceeding the word limit, a real execution cost that lost part of its foundational case. A's closing crystallized the clash more sharply ("who gets paid for the upzone") than B's closing, which mostly restated earlier points.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>A's Rebuttal 2 response to B's ministerial-review defense (A4.5), showing that permit review either preserves the same discretionary fight B claims bans eliminate, or fails to catch cumulative infrastructure overload — a dilemma B's closing did not resolve.</best_rebuttal>
